>Why should the most complicated spec not be the highest dps?  Because then everyone plays one spec and the fact that it's not a hybrid ceases to matter. It's much better to have Destruction, Demon, and Affliction all be within a few thousand DPS of one another as a tradeoff for some specs having certain mechanics over one another. You do **not** want the most complicated spec to flat out be 10% higher damage than any other spec as a pure damage. If that happens, then the other two specs might as well not even exist unless you're okay with playing a subpar spec because you enjoy it. But if that's your mindset then you're probably not a good raider because it means you're intentionally gimping everyone else to have a bit more fun on progression. It also pushes people away from the class because if they dislike the most complex playstyle, they'd rather hop to a new class than play a subpar spec. Plus, you have to compare hybrids vs. pures. All hybrids except Warriors and Death Knights have at most ONE melee and ONE ranged dps spec. You want them to be competitive with the pures so people will bring a Retribution Paladin AND a Rogue instead of two Rogues. But if complexity = damage potential, then the hybrids are artificially gimped because they naturally have fewer options for complexity because they have fewer DPS options period. You get hybrids being pigeonholed into poorly-designed talents like Empowered Seals to remain viable. Complexity directly correlating to damage potential is not healthy for the state of the game.

This equates to 100-140 max hp for str, 60-84 mana for int, and ~ armor and 5-7 AS for agi and equivalent damage loss across the board. So basically if they don't regularly use spells as an int hero, or they're an agi hero outright, this harassment tactic is significantly weaker. Also be mindful against str/int that lowering their max hp/mana means bottle restores more if they bottle up while their stats are low and wait for the debuff to fall off. * The Reactive Armor point is noteworthy for ALL players of this hero, though I always find it debatable how many points to put into Reactive Armor. When I play mid, I always favor a 2/2/1 build that proceeds to max Timber Chain, because I regularly have no survival problems in lane, 2 points in the ultimate enables me to harass a bit harder while also securing more last hits, and maxing Chain facilitates ganks better due to the increased range. If you're being heavily harassed or actively plan on diving often, there is merit in more than 1 Reactive Armor. * The idea of using your ult as a surprise is always a clever thing to do on any hero, but I found it funny here because not only did Badman not set up the ranged creep properly to die, but he also attempted a kill on a mobile hero with a hero that has no lockdown whatsoever. Jump, charge, and be reserved with your dodges. The character can barely dodge at all normally, but he can do a wide quickstep dodge in two situations: 1. When you have your arms charged up. You can quickstep for as long as they remain charged, up to four times in a row with a max-duration charge. 2. Just after landing from a jump, you can quickstep twice in a row. Additionally, you have enough charge duration after landing to dodge once and throw one charged punch. Combined with the fact that the character has very fast-moving and wide jump arcs, and you can very easily jump to the side, land, dodge, and throw out a charged punch to try to sweep around someone. The character is very much about baiting out your opponent's swings and punishing them with a charged hit. Electric-element arms work very well on him because of this, and I'd almost always recommend using one. He has a high-damage grab so a quick electric hit followed by a grab does plenty of damage. Don't spam the grab, just use it to punish in a situation where they can't possibly counter it.

The story of a character, a group, and an item is done, to be sure. But that's just one story they chose to tell in a world that has a lot more potential going on. They left the protagonist's journey open-ended, and the entire first half of the season was more-or-less magical shenanigans completely unrelated to an overarching plot. Moreover, we know *almost nothing* about any of the ancient witches; we know two of their names and we know a little bit about what the two of them did. That still leaves seven of the most important figures in magic history as completely blank slates! We didn't even **see** the school's dungeon in the series despite it being a major setting in the first movie. They've touched on magic theory but they've never spoken of the creation of spells which could lead to an entire story in its own right. The studio confirmed that there are other places of magic study in the world as well as male magic-users, but we saw neither. The main character went through a great deal this season, but she is not done growing - neither as a witch nor as a person. There's still a Macguffin-esque font of magical power sealed in ruins waiting for her to be worthy of it. And with a little bit of planning, the studio could easily continue into a second season with a new story and new mysteries built upon the world they already created. The studio has also apparently stated that they would enjoy working on a second season if given the opportunity. Should they make a second season? That's for them to decide. Could they? Absolutely, quite easily in fact. They left enough open to naturally slot in stories of ancient magic, and strife among the ancient witches, with forbidden secrets locked away in the dungeon, whatever they want to go with.
